Lena demanded that Wes be killed, and Aaron, who had bought a gun for exactly this purpose, was already tracking him toward a motel he'd found through weeks of quiet asking.

Wes Tarrow, before any of that, had been a man remade—born again, sober, holding down a job stacking pallets and coaching boys' baseball on Tuesday nights, though his wife Nita watched him with the particular dread of someone who had seen his old temper and did not entirely believe the new one was permanent.

Lena Ward, in those same years, had been someone else too: a recovered addict who had clawed her way into a suburban life with her husband Doug and their two small daughters, a woman who kept a clean house and did not think much about the years before.

Aaron Vale had a heart that was failing him, a mathematician's heart, and a doctor who told him plainly that without a donor he had weeks left, no more.

By then Lena had already gone back to the needle and the powder, methodically, almost administratively, as if destroying herself were a project with deadlines.

That project had a cause. Wes's pickup struck Doug and both girls at a crossing; he drove on, some instinct turned him back, and then a worse instinct sent him running again.

Before the crash, Della, Aaron's estranged wife, had pressed him to let himself be inseminated with the sperm he'd banked years before, insisting a child should survive him even if he did not survive his heart.

At the hospital, someone in scrubs told Lena that her husband and both of her daughters were dead, and something in her simply stopped functioning as a person and started functioning as a wound.

Wes turned himself in not long after, walking into a police station and confessing, and was sent back to the prison he'd once sworn he'd never see again.

Doug's heart, unclaimed by grief, was given to Aaron, who woke from the surgery alive for the first time in months, astonished at his own pulse.

That aliveness curdled into obsession. Aaron could not stop thinking about whose heart was beating in him, and he hired a private investigator to find the donor's widow.

Wes, released early for good behavior no one quite believed in, walked out on Nita and on the God he'd been so loud about and took a job at a motel far enough away that nobody would recognize him.

Aaron, meanwhile, had followed Lena for weeks before engineering a meeting at a public pool, and what began as reconnaissance became an affair neither of them could name.

He left Della for it, telling her flatly that he did not want the child she was still trying to conceive with his frozen sperm.

At the motel, cornered, Aaron raised the gun he'd bought and could not finish it—he only wounded Wes and told him, absurdly, to run.

Before that, in bed, Aaron had finally told Lena the truth: that he carried her husband's heart inside him. She threw him out that night and took him back before dawn.

Wes, bleeding, did not run far. He followed the two of them back to their motel room and asked Aaron to finish what he'd started, and Aaron, weeping, turned the gun on himself instead.

Lena and Wes together got the dying man to a hospital, where the transplanted heart that had outlived one man failed inside another. Wes went home, finally, to whatever remained of his family, and Lena, pregnant and alone, went home to nothing at all.

The two men in the corner booth of the diner had been talking for maybe six minutes about how broke they were before one of them just stood up, pulled a pistol from his waistband, and announced that everyone should stay calm and empty their pockets. It happened that fast. No plan, no getaway car idling outside, just hunger and a gun and bad math.

Miles away, in a different part of the story that hadn't caught up to this one yet, Rollo and Marcus were crossing the city in a sedan that smelled like an old ashtray, arguing about what a Big Mac was called in France and whether it was true that some countries let you buy heroin at a pharmacy. "That's Amsterdam," Marcus said. "Not everywhere." Rollo didn't believe him.

Later they stood in a dim corridor outside an apartment door, waiting, and Rollo wanted to know if Nadia's foot rubs were worth a man's life. Marcus said nothing was worth that, and then he recited a line of scripture and they went in and shot Tobin dead over a briefcase that wasn't theirs.

They brought the briefcase to Otis's bar, where Otis was in the back room paying a boxer named Denny to lose in the fifth round, sliding bills across a table like the outcome was already history.

That night Rollo bought from Kip, cooked up, and went to find Nadia. They danced under neon at a diner made up like a fifties movie and won the contest, laughing, sweating, alive. Later, on the dealer's floor, she stopped breathing after trying what was in Rollo's pocket, and Kip drove a needle into her chest to bring her back.

Years before any of this, a man freshly released from a prison camp had walked into a stranger's house and placed a gold watch into the hands of a boy who would grow up to be Denny, telling him his father had kept it safe through years he didn't want to describe.

In the ring, that same Denny ignored the money in his pocket, knocked his opponent down and did not stop, and left the arena in the back of a taxi with his hands still wrapped.

In a motel room with the curtains drawn, his girlfriend Marielle admitted she'd left the watch behind at his apartment. He went quiet, looked at the door, said he had to go back for it.

He found Rollo standing at his own kitchen counter, and a submachine gun that had been left there for someone else's use, and used it.

Outside, his car and Otis's collided in the street, and both men woke up bound in the basement beneath a pawnshop.

Denny broke his hands free while one of their captors had Otis pinned to the concrete, and came back swinging a sword pulled off the wall display, and Otis, bleeding, called it even so long as Denny left town for good.

He rode out of the city that night on a stolen motorcycle with Marielle behind him, the watch heavy in his jacket pocket.

Back in that apartment corridor, before any of that, a fourth man had come out of the bathroom firing a revolver that somehow hit nothing, and Marcus called it God's hand moving through the room.

In the car afterward, Rollo's gun went off by accident and took the head off Del in the back seat, and nobody said anything for a long time.

They drove to Warren's house, where a man they didn't know handed them clean shirts and told them exactly how to get blood out of a vinyl seat.

And in the diner, before any of it, the robbery already collapsing, Marcus had talked the gunman down, handed over his own wallet as a kind of toll, kept the briefcase tucked under his arm, and watched the couple walk out the door and vanish into the ordinary morning like nothing at all had happened.

The old man died alone in the great hall of Silvermount, the word "Bluebell" slipping from his lips like the last coin from an upturned purse. The glass snow globe rolled from his fingers and cracked against the marble, and no one heard it fall.

The newsreels came a week later, grainy and solemn, running through the highlights of Emmett Rusk's public life—the papers he'd built, the fortune he'd multiplied, the governor's race he'd lost, the opera house scandal that had scorched every front page in the state. The narrator's voice, brisk and unbothered, noted that his last word had been "Bluebell," and offered no further comment, as if the mystery were beneath the dignity of history.

It was not beneath the dignity of a cub reporter named Nash, who was handed the assignment by an editor amused at his own cruelty. Find out what it means, the editor said. Nash tracked down Nora Kell first, older now and unsteady, singing badly in a seaside nightclub for men who didn't listen. She took one look at him and told him to get out, and did not soften even when he stood in the rain outside for an hour.

So he went further back.

It began, as these things do, with a mother in a mining boarding house signing away her only son. The lodger's mine deed had made the family rich beyond arithmetic, and the banker Barrow wanted the boy as insurance against his own childlessness. She signed. The boy, seven years old and furious, drove his sled into Barrow's stomach before they took him east anyway, sled and all, away from the parents who'd sold him for a signature.

He grew up gilded and cold, and on his twenty-fifth birthday he took the fortune in both hands and told Barrow he wanted, of all the mills and mines and railroads, a dying newspaper called the Clarion. He moved into its offices, brought in Marsh to run the books and Devlin to write what he pleased, and printed a signed statement of principles on the front page like a boy nailing his name to a tree. He stole the whole staff of the rival paper out from under it and threw a party with a brass band and a chorus line to celebrate the theft.

He came home from Europe engaged to Adele, the governor's niece, and for a while there was a marriage that looked like triumph. Then came the breakfasts—weeks of them, months, the two of them behind separate newspapers, the silence thickening like cream gone sour.

He met Nora Kell on a muddy street corner and began visiting her rooms in secret, the way a man visits a version of himself he's forgotten. Mid-campaign for governor, Halloran the party boss brought Adele to those very rooms and threatened to make it public. Emmett refused to withdraw from anything—not the race, not the affair. He lost both. Devlin asked for a transfer. The marriage ended in paperwork.

He married Nora and decided, with the same tyranny he'd brought to the paper, that she would sing opera. She had no voice for it. Devlin, drunk, began the review that damned her, and Emmett—cold, precise—finished it himself and printed it and fired the man who'd started it. Nora swallowed poison rather than sing again, and only then did he let her stop.

He built her a palace, Silvermount, half-finished forever, where she sat with jigsaw puzzles in a hall too large for any voice. After a picnic that curdled into silence, she packed and left him. He wrecked her room afterward and found, among the ruins, a glass snow globe—and said her old nickname, Bluebell, like a man praying to something already gone.

Nash read Barrow's memoir, sat with Marsh, with Devlin, with Nora once she was sober enough to speak, with Colm the butler who'd swept the last of the house. He wrote, in the end, that no single word explains a life—and filed it the same afternoon workmen shoveled a child's rusted sled, marked BLUEBELL in flaking paint, into the furnace.

Tobias skipped work for no reason he could name. He stood on the platform watching his hands shake with a feeling he couldn't place as guilt or hope, then got on the train to the coast anyway. The sand was frozen and empty and there was a woman standing at the edge of it, and something in him leapt before his mind caught up. Her name was Ivy. She said hello like she meant it.

They drove back to the city together, her knee against the gearshift, and she invited him up to her flat like it was the easiest thing in the world.

Weeks later—though he didn't understand yet that it was weeks later, that anything had happened at all—he walked into the bookshop where she worked and she looked at him with the flat politeness of a stranger, laughing at something a young man named Peck had said, her hand near his on the counter. Tobias stood in the doorway feeling erased.

He wasn't wrong. Nina and Grady showed him the letter, a form letter, cold and official, from a clinic that specialized in taking people out of your head. He went straight to the director, a mild man named Dr. Hallam, and demanded they do the same to him.

So he boxed up everything that still smelled like her—a scarf, a ticket stub, a chipped blue mug—so the clinic could map what memories clung to each object. Two technicians came to his flat that night, Dell quiet and clinical, Peck restless, pocketing a bracelet and a photograph when no one was looking, souvenirs for another job.

Inside his own skull, Tobias watched the ugliest, most recent nights dissolve first: the shouting, the silences, the last slammed door. He watched them go and felt lighter and worse.

Then it was Ivy stumbling home drunk, the fender of his car crumpled against the curb, her voice sharp and his silence sharper, and she was gone, coat over one arm, not looking back. The memory before it: month after month of the drinking, the withholding, two people learning exactly which words would bruise.

Back in the flat, Dell and a receptionist named Rosa lay across Tobias's bed passing a joint between them, laughing about nothing, while the machine ran unwatched and the map of his mind buckled off its plotted course.

That was when Tobias reached the memories he loved and refused to let them go. He began smuggling her into scenes she'd never touched—inserting her laugh into a childhood kitchen, her hand into a hospital corridor from before they'd met—hiding her wherever the erasure hadn't reached.

Before that, unraveling backward, there had been two whole years of her: the frozen river, the noodle house steam on the windows, the drive-in with her feet on the dash. Falling, unmistakably, into each other.

Dr. Hallam arrived to correct the drifting map, and Rosa, giddy and reckless, kissed him in the doorway—until his wife appeared and said, quite calmly, that Rosa's affair with him had already been erased once before, that this was the second time she'd forgotten and returned.

Earlier still: the beach party, the empty house at the end of the rail line, breaking a window latch and laughing about it, two strangers becoming something else on a shore in the dark.

The very last memory to survive, glowing at the center of the collapsing map, was that same house, months later, Ivy in the doorway telling him to meet her at the beach, her mouth soft with something like grief.

Then it completed. Tobias woke to an ordinary morning with no Ivy in it at all, no absence he could feel, only an unaccountable itch to skip work.

Months on, Rosa quit the clinic. She mailed out every file, every tape, to every patient on the books, hers included.

Tobias and Ivy sat on her floor and listened to their own recorded voices tearing each other apart, the old cruelties playing back in stereo. She ran. She came back. Sitting across from the wreckage of themselves, they agreed, quietly, to try anyway.

The eggs were cold by the time anyone noticed, and Mr. Birch was still going on about the song on the radio, insisting it wasn't about a girl at all but about heroin, and Cal said that was the stupidest thing he'd ever heard, and the waitress came by to refill coffee and nobody left more than the exact change. Bram said tip her, and Mr. Ash said she didn't do anything but pour, and that was the whole argument, over and over, until the check came.

Elm's blood had soaked through two shirts by the time Ash got him to the warehouse floor, and he held him like a man holding water, saying it over and over, you're not gonna die, you hear me, not gonna die, while Elm screamed and the fluorescent lights buzzed overhead like they didn't care either way.

Birch came through the loading door with his coat flapping, already talking, saying somebody sold them out, said it clean, no hesitation — an informer, had to be, why else would four black-and-whites be sitting on that corner before they'd even cracked the vault. Nobody answered him. He went back out into the lot alone and buried the diamonds under a loose paving stone by the fence, patting the dirt down like a man planting a garden.

That morning, before any of it, Bram had laid the little slips of paper on the table with the names on them — Elm, Ash, Cedar, Birch — and Birch had thrown his back across the table, said he wasn't answering to Birch, sounded like a nancy's dog. Bram told him to pick another tree, then. He picked Birch again out of spite.

Cedar arrived late, grinning, popped his trunk like he was showing off a new car, and there was a cop inside it, wrists zip-tied, mouth taped, blinking against the light. Cedar said his name was Doyle, said he'd been driving too slow past the block and asking too many questions.

Ren Vasco walked out of the gates that same week, blinking in daylight he hadn't earned honestly, and went straight to Bram and Cal, told them he'd kept his mouth shut for six years and now they owed him. Cal said they knew it, and that they'd make it right.

Alone with Doyle, Cedar found a station on the radio, some song from twenty years back, and swayed to it with his eyes shut, then took a knife to the man's ear while he screamed through the tape, and poured gasoline over him slow, humming along.

Elm shot him from the floor where he still lay bleeding, one round through the skull, and told Doyle, gasping through his own pain, that he was police, that there were more outside waiting on Bram.

Weeks before, in a bare room with Pruitt, Danny Roarke had run through the story until it stopped sounding like a lie — the bust in the gas station bathroom, the dealer who begged, all of it rehearsed until it lived in his mouth like memory.

Then the audition, Bram and Cal and Ash listening, nodding, and Bram had said welcome aboard, Mr. Elm.

The robbery itself lasted less than a minute before sirens closed in, and Ash fired his way out the window of the car while Elm crouched low beside him, glass raining down.

On foot, Elm carjacked a stranger who panicked and put a bullet in his gut; Elm killed him for it and kept running, one hand pressed to the wound.

Cal came back to find Cedar dead and Doyle bound and burned, listened to Elm's account without expression, then shot Doyle himself, calm as closing a door.

Bram arrived last, looked at Elm, and said it plain: he's the rat. Ash wouldn't hear it, turned his gun on Bram instead.

It ended in seconds — three men falling, only Ash and Elm left breathing on the concrete.

Elm told him then, finally, that he was a cop, and Ash, weeping, shot him as the doors blew open and the police poured in, and then Ash went down too, under the light of their guns.

The photograph of Roy's ruined face is still curling at the edges when Martin lights a cigarette in the derelict building's doorway. He does not remember shooting him. He only knows the man is dead because the camera says so, because the Polaroid in his hand shows a corpse he apparently made.

He is in a motel room he does not remember checking into, narrating the Prine file down a phone line to a stranger. "Elias Prine," he says. "Claimant. Memory loss, no head trauma on the scans. I called it psychosomatic." He does not know why he is telling this to a voice with no name.

Corinne runs the plate through a friend at the registry and hands him a printout. Roy Mercer. Martin studies the name like it belongs to a stranger, because to him it does.

Weeks — though he cannot count them — before any of this, Elias Prine sits across a desk from him, hands folded, insisting he cannot remember his wife asking him for insulin four times in one evening. Martin denies the claim. He writes malingering in block letters and moves on to the next file.

He drives Vance out past the town limits at gunpoint, the man's nose broken and his shirt soaked through, and leaves him on the shoulder of the highway with the gun still pointed until the shape of him disappears in the mirror.

Elias's wife is already dead by then, cooling in a bed while Elias stands over her with an empty syringe and no memory of using it. It happened, and it will happen, and in Martin's file it is already a closed case, denied, filed.

Corinne hides every pen in the house before she goads him into hitting her, comes back an hour later with a bruise blooming under her eye and Vance's name in her mouth, and Martin writes it into his notes with the little photograph he takes of her face.

He builds his system out of instant film and ink: photographs safety-pinned to motel walls, dates in block capitals, a man's initials — R.M. — tattooed along his forearm so the search cannot be forgotten even when he is.

Corinne serves him a beer the staff have spat in and watches him drink it without knowing, because he recognizes Gil's suit on his own body and Gil's car in the lot outside and something in her wants to make him hurt.

Before that, in the bathroom of his own house, two men come through the door while he is washing his hands. He kills one with the strangers left, and gets the flashlight or the pipe or whatever it is across the skull that undoes the rest of his life.

He drives to a parlor and has a license plate needled into his thigh, sixth fact in a numbered list that will outlast his mind.

He burns his wife's hairbrush in a field because grief needs a fire and he has no way to hold the loss otherwise; he will do this again tomorrow, having forgotten today.

The caller on the phone gives him a name — Gil Marsh — and an address, and Martin writes it on his hand before the ink can fade from his skin.

In the basement he beats Gil until the man cannot speak and photographs what is left.

Gil whispers "Elias" with his last breath, a word Martin cannot place, and he takes the dead man's suit, the dead man's car, and drives.

Roy finds him there, tells him Gil was innocent, that a year ago Martin already killed the real man, that Martin himself is the Prine in his own file.

A year before that, in the dark, Roy had helped him find that real man and watched Martin kill him, a memory that lasted four minutes before it was gone for good.

Martin burns the photographs of Gil instead of believing any of it, writes he is lying to you across Roy's picture, and copies the plate number down as the next name to hunt.

The call came in before dawn, and Detective Isaiah Reece drove to the roadside with his coffee still steaming, thinking it was just another body until he pulled back the sheet and saw his brother's face. Kwame. Burned around the edges, dumped like trash. Reece stood there a long time before he could make himself speak into the radio.

Weeks earlier, before any of that, Nadir had walked into a gun shop with his daughter Sahar beside him, and the dealer behind the counter had repeated his words back in a mocking accent, sliding the pistol across the counter like he was doing him a favor.

Not long after, two young men, Trey and Kwame, forced open the door of a car outside a restaurant and pushed the prosecutor Halstead out onto the curb, driving off with his keys still warm in the ignition.

A locksmith named Mateo came to fix the Halsteads' locks after that, and Paula stood in the doorway insisting to her husband that this man, this stranger, was probably casing the house for his friends.

Around the same time, Officer Boyle stopped a couple named the Hobarts on a dark road, and what he did to Renee in front of her husband Clay was the kind of thing that doesn't leave a person, though he let them drive on with only a warning.

His partner Voss couldn't stomach another shift beside him after that, and asked their commander for a new car, if not a new partner.

Mateo, still working, replaced the lock on a shop belonging to Nadir, warned him plainly that the door itself was rotted through and wouldn't hold — and Nadir, suspicious of everyone by then, called him a con man to his face.

Boyle, meanwhile, sat across from an insurance clerk named Delia Frank, begging for coverage for his dying father, and was refused with a shrug and a form letter.

Nadir's shop was gutted that same week, looted in the night, and when he filed the claim the insurer pointed to the ignored warning about the door and refused to pay a cent.

Trey and Kwame, still running wild, ran down a shopkeeper named Pham with their car and left him bleeding on the curb outside a hospital, driving off without looking back.

Later, Renee was trapped upside down in a burning wreck, and it was Boyle — the same officer — who crawled through fire and glass to drag her out by the arms.

Clay, desperate and furious, was caught mid-carjacking of his own stolen car, and it was Voss who stood between him and the guns of other officers, talking them down one word at a time.

Clay sped off with Trey inside, driving hard through red lights before finally throwing him out onto the pavement and disappearing.

Nadir, certain now that Mateo had ruined him, waited outside the locksmith's house with the gun from the shop, and fired just as Mateo's small daughter Rosie ran laughing into her father's arms.

The bullet found nothing. Sahar had swapped the rounds for blanks without telling him, and Nadir, shaking, decided the girl was his angel, sent to stop him.

Voss, driving alone that same season, picked up a hitchhiker who reached into his pocket — and shot him dead before he understood what he'd done. He burned the car afterward, telling himself it was nothing.

That hitchhiker was Kwame, and it was Reece's own mother who told him afterward, voice flat with grief, that he had never once gone looking for his brother, not even when he vanished for weeks at a time.

Paula, humbled by then, fell down her own staircase and lay there until Alba found her, and when she finally spoke, it was to say that Alba was the only friend she had left in the world.

Trey, alone now, found the back of Pham's van stacked with frightened migrants meant for sale, and instead of selling them himself, he drove to the docks and let them go into the night.

And when the first snow came that year, two strangers collided on an icy street corner, and stood there shouting at each other, breath rising white into the cold, as if none of it had ever happened before.

The car came apart like something breathing its last, glass fogging red, and Ruben's forehead cracked the windshield of a life he'd already ruined twice over.

Before that, there had been the house. Cramped, four walls holding his mother, his brother Nestor, Nestor's wife Alma, their baby, and Ruben himself, all of them stacked like crates in a warehouse. Nestor came home some nights smelling of other men's pharmacies, and his hands found Alma the way they found the cash register — hard, practiced. Ruben started telling her to run. Just leave, he'd whisper, I'll take you and the baby somewhere he can't reach.

It was around then Ruben found out what Tigre was — Nestor's rottweiler, gentle at the foot of the bed until another dog wandered close, and then not gentle at all. Ruben started entering him in the pits behind the tannery. The dog won and won.

He paid two men to break Nestor's ribs for what he'd done to Alma. Nestor didn't stay to be broken twice. He took Alma, the baby, and the money Ruben had hidden in a coffee tin, and was gone before sunrise.

In the ring, months later, the promoter Chaco put a bullet in Tigre rather than pay out. Ruben put a knife in Chaco. He and Pipo ran into the dark with the dog bleeding out behind them, and that's how Ruben came to be driving too fast through a red light, colliding with the life of a woman he'd never meet properly.

Nestor died first, though — shot climbing out of a bank he had no business robbing. At the funeral Ruben asked Alma one more time. She looked at the coffin, not at him, and said no.

Celine Vaz didn't know any of these people. Her lover Hector had left his wife and daughters for her, moved her into a flat with her own face forty feet tall on the billboard outside the window. She woke in a hospital bed after the crash with a pinned leg and a missing dog — Chispa, her lapdog, gone into the walls of the new apartment like a rumor. Hector tore up the floorboards looking for it while Celine's leg turned black at the edges. They took the leg. Later they took the billboard down too, peeled her smile off the building in long strips.

A man named Cardo was at that junction the night of the crash — a former guerrilla who killed for money now, homeless by choice or ruin, hard to say which. He dragged the dying dog out of Ruben's wreckage because it was the only thing there worth saving.

Elian, a businessman, hired Cardo not long after to kill his half-brother Sergio. Before that job, Cardo had stood far off at his estranged wife's burial, then followed his grown daughter Perla home just to see the shape of the life he'd left her.

He nursed the dog — Tigre — back from the edge among his own pack of strays. Then one day he came home to find Tigre had killed them all, every stray, silent and thorough. He put the gun to the dog's skull and his hand would not do it.

He took Sergio instead of killing him, chained him in his lair. Brought Elian to look at his own brother's face, left a loaded pistol on the table between them, and walked out with money from both men in his pocket.

He broke into Perla's flat once more, left his whole ugly history on her answering machine, and stole a photograph of her from the wall.

Then he shaved, put on clean clothes, left every peso he had folded on her table, and walked out past the city's edge into the wasteland, Tigre loping quiet at his heel, the two of them the only things left standing from all that wreckage.

The gun tastes like a socket wrench and copper, and my cheek opens like a mouth that wasn't invented yet. I go down against the stairwell wall, and the man wearing my face slides off me for good, and I understand, with the particular clarity of blood loss, that I have finally killed him.

But that's later. That's the top floor of a building that hasn't fallen yet in this telling.

I should start with the sleeplessness, since that's where he started.

I hadn't slept without help in years. The only thing that worked was crying — real crying, shoulders-shaking crying — at support groups for diseases I did not have. Testicular cancer on Tuesdays. Blood parasites on Thursdays. I sat in circles of folding chairs and grieved for organs I still owned.

Then Ada Vey started coming. She faked it so badly, dry-eyed, checking her phone, that she made a fraud of my one clean thing.

Before any of that, on a business flight, I sat next to a soap salesman named Rex Marrow, and pocketed his card without thinking much of it.

My apartment blew up not long after — the catalogue furniture, the particleboard, all of it gone — and I called the only number I had left. Rex took me into a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district and told me I could stay.

Outside a bar one night he asked me to hit him as hard as I could. I did. We beat each other bloody in the car park under a security light, and something in me finally exhaled.

It became weekly. A basement. Rules nobody wrote down but everybody obeyed. More men kept arriving, like word had gotten out through skin.

Ada overdosed and Rex carried her into the house himself, and after that they had a loud, ugly affair I couldn't stand listening to through the walls.

Rex was rendering fat — stolen from a cosmetic surgery clinic — into soap, and selling it back to department stores for eighty dollars a bar. I told him it was insane. He told me everything was.

He burned my hand with lye once and held it there when I tried to leave my body the way I knew how, meditating myself out of the pain. "Stay," he said. "This is the part that's real."

I blackmailed my employer with my own beaten face — paid to disappear, essentially — and used the money to disappear further into whatever this was becoming.

Rex named it Havoc. The house filled with shaven heads, boys taking orders, vandalizing storefronts and vans with a discipline that frightened me.

Then he drove us into oncoming traffic, let the car roll twice, and walked away from the wreck laughing, and I didn't see him again.

A member named Ogden got shot on an operation I hadn't approved, and I started trying to tear the whole organization down with my hands.

I went city to city looking for the source of it and found the same clubs everywhere, the same shaven men greeting me like a returning king. "Rex," they said. "Rex Marrow."

I worked it out on a bus at four in the morning: there was no Rex. There was only me, awake in the daylight and someone else entirely at night, wearing my hands.

Ada didn't even flinch when I told her. "I know," she said. "It was always you."

Havoc had mined the towers of the debt-record companies — I found the charges myself, tried to cut wires with fingers that weren't steady.

Which brings us back to the stairwell, the gun, the second mouth I gave myself to end him.

Afterward the recruits, still loyal to whoever survived, brought Ada up through the smoke. We stood at the window holding hands while the towers came down floor by floor, glass raining sideways, and for the first time in years I felt something close enough to rest.

The old man's flat overlooked the street, and he was explaining to the younger one, his nephew, that nothing survives time. Not stone, not love, not the shape of a face you thought you'd memorized. "Everything erodes," he said, tapping ash into a saucer. "Even the worst nights. Even the men who caused them."

Below, on the pavement, blue lights washed the brick in pulses. Two men were being carried out of a club called the Pit, handcuffed, their shirts torn, their faces slack with the particular exhaustion that comes after violence has finished with you. The old man watched without much interest, as if he'd seen a hundred such scenes from this window and expected a hundred more.

Inside the club, minutes before, Jonah had swung a fire extinguisher into a stranger's face until the man's features stopped resembling a face at all, while a few feet away the real Adder stood watching, arms folded, untouched, almost curious. Before that, Cort had seized the wrong man entirely, some clubgoer with bad luck and a leather jacket, and snapped his arm at the elbow with a sound like a branch giving way.

Before that, two men on the street outside had offered, for a price, to sell Cort the name of the man who'd hurt Lise, and had steered him and Jonah toward the Pit with the easy confidence of men who did this often.

All night the helicopters passed low over the rooftops, spraying for the pests that had gotten into the almond trees, their searchlights sweeping bedroom windows before moving on to the next block, and the next, until every neighbourhood had been dusted with the same fine chemical rain.

Neil Hartigan buttoned his shirt while his wife Bess stood at the mirror doing something complicated with her hair, and neither of them heard the helicopters at all, absorbed as they were in the small logistics of a dinner party — wine, candles, whether the Delacroix print looked pretentious over the mantel.

Across town Cheryl sat in her living room with the phone cradled against her shoulder, murmuring to a stranger about a cabin and snow while her husband Stu sat three feet away pretending to read, his jaw working like a man chewing glass.

Vida was already at the club, testing the microphone, her voice curling up into the rafters, while at home her daughter Bee sat with her cello between her knees and played to no one, the empty apartment swallowing the notes whole.

Officer Rowe told his wife Peg he had an early shift. He drove instead to Nan's, and on the way out the door he let the dog slip its collar and did not look back to see if it followed.

Charlie Rill was walking to school when Rhona's car came around the corner too fast; he went down hard, got up, brushed off his knees, and told his mother at the door that he was fine, completely fine.

That same week the baker Otto Kemp took down an order in his ledger: a birthday cake, blue icing, for a boy named Charlie Rill.

By evening Charlie was in a coma, and Grant and Elaine sat on either side of his bed under the fluorescent lights, holding his still hands.

The Hartigans' house sat empty except for Ike and Dot, who were meant to be watering plants and instead spent an afternoon posing Dot on the kitchen floor in smeared red paint, Ike circling her with the camera, laughing at how convincing the corpse looked.

Downriver, Stu and three friends waded out with their rods and found a woman floating face down among the reeds, her hair fanned out like something growing.

Not far from there, in a small rented room, Cass took a saw to Nan's furniture, working methodically through the legs of a table, the arm of a chair, because he'd heard she had someone new and could not think what else to do with his hands.

At the hospital, Otto's unpaid invoices piled up on his counter, and in the nights that followed he began calling the Rill house, saying nothing at first, then things meant to frighten.

The men tied the body to a root at the river's edge and kept fishing for two more days before anyone thought to call it in.

Grant's father Duff, absent for twenty years, appeared at the hospital doors and, standing over his dying grandson, confessed an affair from decades before, as if confession now could balance anything.

Iris, who clowned at children's parties for a living, heard what her husband Vern had done at the river and could not look at him afterward.

At the dinner party, wine loosened Bess's tongue, and she told the table about a nude modelling session years ago, and then, worse, about the affair; Neil stood so fast his chair fell backward.

Charlie died a few days later. Grant and Elaine drove to the bakery to confront the man who'd been calling, but found Otto weeping over the ovens, and he fed them warm bread and wept with them instead.

Bee found her mother asleep on the couch, closed the garage door quietly, and sat in the car with the engine running.

At a picnic in the hills, sun-drunk and furious at nothing anyone could name, Stu picked up a rock and brought it down on a young woman's skull.

That evening the ground shook once, hard, rattling glasses off shelves across the city, and the late news gathered every death, every wreck, every quiet ruin into a single scrolling bulletin, as if it had all happened at once.

Solly Two Coats and his crew went into the diamond house in the northern port dressed as pilgrims, hymnals tucked under their arms, and walked out with a stone the size of a walnut. Nobody in that town would ever be that devout again.

Across the water, Halloway and Digby had sent their fighter Pretty Sam down to a travellers' camp to buy a caravan, thinking it a small errand. It wasn't. Finn, a bare-knuckle man with hands like shovels, put Sam on the ground over the price of a wheel and left him there dreaming. That same week Solly's cousin Marv rang through and told him not to sit on the stone — bring it straight over, now, no delays.

With Sam concussed and useless, Halloway had no fighter for Coldstone's fixed bout, so he put Finn in instead, swearing to Coldstone that the big man would go down clean in the fourth round. Coldstone didn't like surprises, but he liked money more, and took the bet.

Meanwhile Grigor the Nail, always working two ends of a rope, told Solly about a soft bookmaker's shop worth robbing in the city — and in the same breath tipped off the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno to hit the very same place. Grigor liked watching things collide.

Solly landed in the city, handed the stone to the fence Hersch for safekeeping, and went off to the bookmaker's to put money on the fight he'd heard was fixed. Finn, however, flattened his man in the first round instead of the fourth, and Coldstone, out a fortune, turned his fury on Halloway. At the same shop, Ike, Benno and a driver called Tulley bungled their robbery badly, grabbing Solly's arm and his case for a case, only to be chased off into the night by Grigor himself.

Marv flew in behind the mess, found his cousin vanished and the stone unaccounted for, and hired a bounty hunter named Ledge to hunt him down. Grigor got there first — took Solly, cut the arm off him to open the case, and found the stone wasn't even inside it. Furious, Coldstone had Solly's remains fed to his pigs and warned Halloway and Digby exactly what would happen if the next fight went wrong too.

Ledge, meanwhile, traced the pawnbrokers to their car, shot it to ribbons, and dragged Ike and Benno out along with the stone they'd been sitting on the whole time.

Halloway and Digby told Finn again — fourth round, no earlier — and that night Coldstone's men burned Finn's mother alive in her caravan to make sure the message landed. It landed.

Grigor, never able to leave well enough alone, ambushed Ledge's car with Ike and Benno still inside it. In the shootout that followed, Ledge, Grigor, and Benno all died in the road, and in the confusion, Tulley slipped away with the camp dog — the same dog that had, quite by accident, swallowed the diamond whole.

Finn fought again, knocked his man cold in the fourth exactly as promised, and while the crowd was still roaring, the travellers came down through the seats and slaughtered Coldstone's men where they sat. Halloway and Digby found Coldstone himself cowering by the ring steps and shot him there. By morning the travellers had folded their camp and vanished like they'd never come.

Weeks later, a stray dog was handed in at a pet shop across town, coughed up a walnut-sized stone onto the counter, and the shopkeeper called the two names still written on its collar tag. Halloway and Digby came to collect the dog and left holding, of all things, the diamond that had cost so many men their lives.

In the bar, two years afterwards, Odile turned the stem of her glass and told Wilder that her marriage was over. She said she had spent the previous night confessing everything to Emlyn, sitting up until the fire went out, telling him things she had not admitted even to herself in the telling. Wilder listened with the stillness of a man waiting for a verdict that concerned him.

Then, almost as an afterthought, she mentioned that Emlyn had been publishing a writer named Cazalet, a man both of them had always quietly despised for his adjectives and his self-regard, and that this had come up somehow in the course of the night, a small absurd detail among the large ones.

Wilder rang Emlyn that same hour, his voice thin with something between guilt and outrage, and Emlyn came round in the evening, unhurried, hat still on when he sat down.

"I've known for four years," Emlyn said, settling into the chair as though it were an ordinary visit. "She told me on the trip abroad. And I never thought much of your letters either, if we're confessing things tonight."

Before that telling — long before — there had been the rooms. Wilder and Odile had decided, without much ceremony, that the rented rooms had become a chore. They split the crockery between them on the kitchen table, dividing plates and cups with the seriousness of people settling an estate, and surrendered the lease to a landlord who did not ask why.

There had been, too, the dinners at the married house, where Emlyn and Wilder talked only of racquets and schoolboy sport, of nets and courts and old matches, until Odile sat with her wine and had no part in the talk at all, a guest in her own dining room.

And before that, the hotel abroad, where Emlyn had asked at the desk about a letter held for her, addressed in a hand he recognised at once, the loops of it too familiar to be anyone else's. Odile confessed there, in the hotel room with the shutters half-drawn, and Emlyn had only remarked, mildly, that he had always been fonder of his friend than of his wife — said it the way one might remark on weather, without cruelty, as if it settled something rather than broke it.

She went back to the rented rooms afterward and said nothing whatever about the trip. The afternoon passed exactly as the others had, the tea things laid out, the window open on the quiet street, as though nothing in the world had shifted.

Emlyn, for his part, took Wilder to a long lunch at a restaurant with white cloths and drank through it steadily, baiting him gently about contemporary fiction, about the flatness of new novels and the laziness of new novelists, and never once mentioned what he had learned. Wilder laughed along, unaware of the knowledge sitting across the table from him like an uninvited guest.

Earlier still, the rooms themselves had been furnished — Wilder and Odile filling them with linen and plates, giving the affair a household of its own, curtains chosen, a kettle bought, a life built in miniature that answered to no one.

And there had been the day Odile said she was carrying her husband's child, said it quietly over the little table they had bought together, and the two of them had decided, without much discussion, that the rented rooms would go on exactly as before, as though a child changed nothing about linen and plates and afternoons.

All of it had begun at a party, at the house of Wilder's closest friend, where Wilder had led Odile up a back stairway to a room above the noise and told her, quite simply, how lovely she was, while below them the other guests went on drinking, unaware that anything above their heads had started at all.

He became unstuck in time, as he liked to say, and so the war found him first as a chaplain's assistant, shipped overseas with no training worth the name, carrying a Bible he did not understand for a God he was not sure of. Then, without transition, he was in the zoo on Zircon-211, behind glass, with a former film actress who paced the false grass and asked him questions he could not answer, while small crowds of aliens with hands like shy stars watched them eat and sleep and not quite touch.

He was born, after that, in a small industrial town, and grew into a weak, peculiar child who flinched at loud noises and dreamed with his eyes open. He was sent on to a great city and housed with other prisoners in a disused abattoir, sleeping among the hooks and the cold smell of old blood, waiting for orders that never explained themselves.

He came home, collapsed, and was hospitalised. In the next bed was a man who introduced him to a hack science fiction writer, a man with visionary teeth and a suitcase full of paperbacks about time and other planets, who talked to him kindly, as if he already believed everything that was coming.

The aliens explained, in their flat, patient way, that every moment exists at once, that his idea of free will was a peculiarity of his own small blue planet, and that nothing could be otherwise than it was. He nodded as if this were reasonable, because by then it was.

He was lost behind the lines with a scout who beat him for wanting to be left to die in the snow, calling him useless, calling him worse.

He married the daughter of the man who owned the optometry school and became rich, moving into a house with white columns and a maid who called him sir without irony, as though money could smooth over the parts of him that did not fit.

The city was destroyed by fire in one night, and he came up from the meat locker with the others to find it gone—a flat, smoking plain where a city had been, everything erased at once, all times equally present in the ash.

His daughter decided he was senile and took his affairs out of his hands, speaking to him gently, the way one speaks to something already lost.

His father threw him into the deep end of the pool to teach him to swim, and he sank to the bottom, and lay there, and did not fight it, because some part of him already knew he would rise again into some other year.

The scout died of gangrene on the prison train, blaming him with his last rattling breath, as though blame were a debt that could be called in from any direction, forward or back.

He went on a radio talk show and tried to tell the world about the aliens and the fourth dimension, about the zoo and the film actress and the moment that never ends, and the host smiled at him the way people smile at something breakable.

The prisoners were made to dig bodies out of the cellars until one of the diggers died of the dry heaves, folding over in the ash and not getting up again, and no one stopped digging.

He survived an air crash in the mountains, and his wife died of exhaust fumes driving to the hospital to see him, and he learned of it lying in a hospital bed of his own, in a year that felt, to him, exactly as present as any other.

He was held in a camp beside enemy officers who had been drawing double rations for years through a clerical error, fat and embarrassed among the starving, apologizing without ever giving it back.

He was shot dead by a beam weapon after addressing a crowd, exactly as he had always known he would be, and did not flinch, because he had seen it already, the way he had seen everything already, all of it at once, always.

A fellow prisoner, somewhere in there, in no order he could name, promised to have him killed one day on the dead scout's account, and he only nodded, because he already knew that too.

His daughter decided he was senile and took his affairs out of his hands, speaking to him gently, the way one speaks to something already lost.

His father threw him into the deep end of the pool to teach him to swim, and he sank to the bottom, and lay there, and did not fight it, because some part of him already knew he would rise again into some other year.

The scout died of gangrene on the prison train, blaming him with his last rattling breath, as though blame were a debt that could be called in from any direction, forward or back.

He went on a radio talk show and tried to tell the world about the aliens and the fourth dimension, about the zoo and the film actress and the moment that never ends, and the host smiled at him the way people smile at something breakable.

The prisoners were made to dig bodies out of the cellars until one of the diggers died of the dry heaves, folding over in the ash and not getting up again, and no one stopped digging.

He survived an air crash in the mountains, and his wife died of exhaust fumes driving to the hospital to see him, and he learned of it lying in a hospital bed of his own, in a year that felt, to him, exactly as present as any other.

He was held in a camp beside enemy officers who had been drawing double rations for years through a clerical error, fat and embarrassed among the starving, apologizing without ever giving it back.

He was shot dead by a beam weapon after addressing a crowd, exactly as he had always known he would be, and did not flinch, because he had seen it already, the way he had seen everything already, all of it at once, always.

A fellow prisoner, somewhere in there, in no order he could name, promised to have him killed one day on the dead scout's account, and he only nodded, because he already knew that too.
